title: WATER in 10 languages: say it, spell it, remember it
title_variants: How to say WATER in 10 languages
WATER: Mandarin, Hindi, Spanish and 7 more
Learn WATER in 10 languages in 5 minutes
description: One everyday English word a day, in ten of the world's most spoken languages. Today: water. Hear it, see the script, learn a memory hook and one cultural note per language.
intro: Today's word is water. You will say it more often than almost any other noun when you travel: at a cafe, in a shop, at a station. Here is water in ten languages, with a memory hook and one cultural note for each. Say each one out loud.
outro: That is water in ten languages. Mandarin shui, Hindi pani, Spanish agua, French eau, Bengali pani, Portuguese agua, Russian voda, Urdu pani, Japanese mizu, Italian acqua. Which one surprised you? Tell us in the comments. Subscribe for one new word every day.

languages.memory_hook: Shway: picture water swaying in a glass, with the voice dipping down and up on the third tone.
languages.cultural_note: Hot water, rè shuǐ, is the default drink in much of China; ask for bīng shuǐ if you want it cold.
languages.narrator_intro: Number one, Mandarin. Water is shuǐ.
languages.narrator_wrap: Think of water swaying in a glass: shway. The tone dips down and rises up, like the sway. In much of China the default drink is hot water, rè shuǐ, so ask for bīng shuǐ, ice water, if you want it cold.

languages.memory_hook: Pānī sounds like a pony: picture a pony drinking a long, cool drink of water.
languages.cultural_note: Jal is the formal or poetic word, used on signs and in prayers; pānī is what everyone says at the table.
languages.narrator_intro: Number two, Hindi. Water is pānī.
languages.narrator_wrap: Pānī sounds like pony. Picture a pony drinking a long, cool drink of water. You will see jal on signs and hear it in prayers, because it is the formal word, but pānī is what everyone says at the table.

languages.example_english: I want a glass of water.
languages.memory_hook: Agua is the start of aquarium: a tank full of water.
languages.cultural_note: Agua is feminine but takes el in the singular, el agua, because of the stressed a; it is still las aguas in the plural.
languages.narrator_intro: Number three, Spanish. Water is agua.
languages.narrator_wrap: Agua is the start of aquarium, a tank full of water. One trap: agua is feminine, but you say el agua, not la agua, because the word begins with a stressed a. In the plural it goes back to las aguas.

languages.example_native: Je voudrais de l'eau, s'il vous plaît.
languages.example_romanised: Je voudrais de l'eau, s'il vous plaît.
languages.example_english: I would like some water, please.
languages.memory_hook: Three letters, one sound: eau is just oh, like the oh you say when you spill it.
languages.cultural_note: In a French restaurant une carafe d'eau is free tap water; eau minérale is bottled and costs money.
languages.narrator_intro: Number four, French. Water is eau.
languages.narrator_wrap: Three letters, one sound. Eau is just oh, like the oh you say when you spill it. In a French restaurant ask for une carafe d'eau and you get free tap water. Eau minérale is the bottled kind, and it costs money.

languages.memory_hook: Same pony as Hindi: pani, a pony drinking water, now in Bengali.
languages.cultural_note: Bangladesh and Muslim Bengalis mostly say pani; in West Bengal you will more often hear jol for the same water.
languages.narrator_intro: Number five, Bengali. Water is pani.
languages.narrator_wrap: The same pony as Hindi: pani, a pony drinking water, now in Bengali. There is a regional split. In Bangladesh most people say pani. Across the border in West Bengal you will more often hear jol, and both mean exactly the same water.

languages.memory_hook: Água looks like Spanish agua with a hat on the first a: that accent marks the stress.
languages.cultural_note: In Brazil água com gás is sparkling and água sem gás is still; most cafes ask which one you want.
languages.narrator_intro: Number six, Portuguese. Water is água.
languages.narrator_wrap: Água looks like the Spanish word with a small hat on the first a. That accent tells you where the stress goes: AH gwa. In Brazil you will be asked com gás or sem gás, with bubbles or without, almost every time you order it.

languages.example_english: Can I have some water, please?
languages.memory_hook: Vodá is where vodka comes from: vodka literally means little water.
languages.cultural_note: Russians often stress the last syllable, va-DA; the unstressed o sounds like a soft a, so it is not vo-da.
languages.narrator_intro: Number seven, Russian. Water is vodá.
languages.narrator_wrap: Vodá is where vodka comes from. Vodka literally means little water. Put the stress on the end, va-DA, and let the first o soften into an a. Say vo-DA with a clear o and people will hear the accent straight away.

languages.memory_hook: The same pony again: Urdu and Hindi share the spoken word, only the script changes.
languages.cultural_note: Urdu is written right to left in Nastaliq; the printed word looks different from Hindi's Devanagari but sounds the same.
languages.narrator_intro: Number eight, Urdu. Water is pānī.
languages.narrator_wrap: The same pony one more time. Urdu and Hindi share the spoken word pānī. What changes is the script. Urdu runs right to left in the flowing Nastaliq style, so the word on screen looks nothing like the Hindi one, but it sounds exactly the same.

languages.memory_hook: Mizu: picture mist rising from water in the morning.
languages.cultural_note: In restaurants ask for omizu; the polite o makes it sound natural, and cold water usually arrives free.
languages.narrator_intro: Number nine, Japanese. Water is mizu.
languages.narrator_wrap: Mizu. Picture mist rising from water in the morning. In a Japanese restaurant say omizu, with a polite o in front, and a glass of cold water usually arrives for free. The same character is used for water in Chinese, read shuǐ there.

languages.memory_hook: Acqua is aqua with a c: the hard c-q makes the k sound long, AK-kwa.
languages.cultural_note: Waiters ask naturale o frizzante, still or sparkling; tap water is rarely served in Italian restaurants.
languages.narrator_intro: Number ten, Italian. Water is acqua.
languages.narrator_wrap: Acqua is aqua with an extra c. That double consonant makes the k sound long: AK-kwa. In Italy the waiter will ask naturale o frizzante, still or sparkling, because bottled water is the norm and tap water is rarely served at the table.
